Week
1 focuses on lowering baseline arousal and establishing two foundational skills indoors—
voluntary eye contact on cue and understanding the dog's threshold distance. I'm planning
two short daily sessions plus a sniffari, with specific exercises like the name game for
check-ins, hand targeting, scatter "find it" games as a
low-cost disengagement tool, and longer decompression sniff walks on a long line to naturally
lower arousal. The critical management rule throughout all four weeks is eliminating nose-to-nose greetings on le
ash entirely, since every greeting reinforces frustration. I'll test the threshold distance by
parking at various distances from dog traffic and noting where he notices without barking, then move

to week 2 once he's hitting 8 out of 10 marked check-ins in the front yard.

Week 2
shifts to loose-leash mechanics and the foundational leash rule—
when
tension appears, I stop completely with feet planted until slack returns,
then resume walking as the reward. I'm also using a "1
-2-3" pattern game that gives a predictable rhythm and keeps his head up, plus reverse direction as a penalty. The training
walk progression moves from hallway to driveway to quiet cul-de-sac to mildly busy streets, always avoiding the trigger
-rich route, and I'm splitting the training walk from the daily exercise walk so they serve
different purposes. He passes week 2 once he can maintain 20 consecutive slack-leash steps on the quiet street for

three days running.

Week 3 introduces the dog trigger deliberately at threshold distance—I'll sit
on a bench at a park path or similar spot with the
dog behind a visual barrier if needed, and mark the moment he notices another dog.
Reduce
distance by 10-20% only when the previous distance feels easy over three consecutive
sessions, then gradually reintroduce moving dogs through parallel walking at distance. On
real walks, the moment a dog appears, increase distance and mark-and-feed while continuing forward—the goal is a clean
pass, not an interaction. By end of week 4, he should
pass a dog across a residential street without sustained barking at least half the time. Equally
important: a border collie needs a solid baseline of enrichment—
two food puzzles daily, a 15-minute training session, and safe off-leash decompression—because chronic high arousal blocks
learning, and adolescent dogs also need adequate sleep.

a simple log to track progress, and be realistic: four
weeks gets a noticeably bigger threshold distance and a walkable leash, but ign
oring dogs entirely takes three to six months. I'll organize this
as weekly subtasks under the main task so the structure shows the progression, assigned
